**On Attention**

Somewhere across a loud room, someone says your name. The party snaps into a different shape. A second ago the noise was a single gray roar; now it has depth, channels, a direction. And you realize, with a small start, that your ear had been filtering all of it the whole time — that everything you didn't hear was being actively unheard. Attention, it turns out, is not something you do when you decide to listen. It is something that was already being done, in the dark, on your behalf, all along.

William James began his chapter on attention in 1890 with a shrug disguised as a definition. Everyone knows what attention is, he wrote: the taking possession by the mind, "in clear and vivid form," of one out of what seem several simultaneously possible objects or trains of thought. The shrug is the point. Attention is the one mental act so close to us that describing it feels like describing the act of describing. James also gave us the infant, "assailed by eyes, ears, nose, skin, and entrails at once," experiencing it all as one great blooming, buzzing confusion. Attention is the education of that confusion. It is how the buzzing gets carved into a world — this face, that word, this room, that threat. You were not born into a world. You were born into noise, and attention is the slow, lifelong sculpting of that noise into everything you have ever known.

Two things follow, and the first is slightly alarming. If attention carves the world, then what you don't attend to doesn't just go unnoticed — it fails, in a meaningful sense, to fully exist for you. In 1999, Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris asked people to count basketball passes in a short video, and partway through, a person in a gorilla suit strolled through the frame. Roughly half of viewers never saw the gorilla. What's unsettling is not the miss but the confidence beforehand. Ask anyone whether they would notice a gorilla walking through a basketball game, and they laugh. The gorilla study is really a study of hubris. We move through our days certain that the world is fully there, streaming into us, and that attention is merely a flashlight we occasionally aim. It is closer to the reverse. Attention is the knife that cuts a world out of the flood, and everything the knife doesn't cut flows on without us.

The second thing that follows is better news: attention is trainable, and training it makes the world bigger. For decades, Japan ran schools for chick sexing — sorting day-old chicks by sex, a commercially urgent and astonishingly subtle task. Apprentices would watch a master work, and the master would say only "yes" or "no." No one could articulate the rule. There may not have been a rule — just a pattern of down and vent shape too fine for language, lodged in the master through thousands of small corrections. After months, something uncanny happened: the apprentice would look at a chick and simply see it. Not deduce. See. The knowledge never existed anywhere except in attention, and it could be transmitted only through contact with someone else's attention.

You can find the same story in any trained perception. Radiologists, after years of reading scans, come to see lesions the way the rest of us see a friend's face in a crowd — instantly, whole — and imaging studies suggest their visual cortices respond to things a novice's simply doesn't. Birders know the moment when a song goes from being part of the generic morning hum to being a specific someone with a specific address. The white-throated sparrow sings what Americans hear as "Poor Sam Peabody, Peabody, Peabody" — Canadians, with more civic pride, hear "O sweet Canada, Canada, Canada." Learn that song once and you will hear it everywhere, in parking lots, behind movie dialogue, for the rest of your life. The world did not change. Your attention did, and the world got bigger inside it.

William Blake, scolding a disappointed patron, wrote: "The tree which moves some to tears of joy is in the eyes of others only a green thing which stands in the way." That is a description of the ladder of attention — rung after rung, a lifetime of noticing — and it is not clear that the ladder has a top. Somewhere above the casual listener is the birder; above the birder is the person who knows individual sparrows; above that, whoever attends so finely that the boundary between the watcher and the watched begins to thin.

If attention builds the world, it is only a short step — but a strange one — to the claim that attention is the whole of ethics. Simone Weil took that step. "Attention," she wrote to a friend in 1942, "is the rarest and purest form of generosity." She meant it with the terrible precision she meant everything. Weil had worked in factories and vineyards deliberately, to learn what affliction does to a person, and she noticed that the suffering do not ask first for solutions. They ask to be seen. Pity, advice, even help can land like a slap from someone who has not attended. What the afflicted need, she thought, is the miracle of being accurately noticed. Attention, because it costs the giver the most finite thing they have and asks nothing of the receiver, was the purest gift she could name.

Weil also made the strangest and best argument in the philosophy of education. A student struggling with a geometry problem she cannot solve, who keeps returning to it without cheating or collapsing into distraction, has gained something even in failure: the effort itself is nourishment. And then the sentence that stops you: "Attention, taken to its highest degree, is the same thing as prayer." This sounds mystical until you try it. Hold one small thing in mind — a problem, a line of poetry, a person's difficult remark — and refuse to flinch off it or fog it over, and you discover how rarely you can do it, and how much happens when you can. To attend, unmixed, for its own sake, to something other than yourself: what else would we call that?

Iris Murdoch took Weil's idea and gave it a plot. In *The Sovereignty of Good*, she imagines a mother, M, who dislikes her daughter-in-law, D. To M, D is common, trivial, loud. M is a decent person; she never says any of it; her behavior is impeccable. But over time, unadvertised and unheroic, M revises her view. She comes to see D as young, spontaneous, not common at all — and here is Murdoch's kicker: D has not changed. Nothing happened. No act was performed, no apology made, no resolve undertaken. There was only a slow, laborious correction of vision. Murdoch believed this was the real location of the moral life — not in dramatic choices under pressure, but in the daily work of seeing justly. "I can only choose within the world I can see," she wrote, and love, in her hardest and best definition, is "the extremely difficult realisation that something other than oneself is real."

If Murdoch is right, then the moral life mostly happens in perception, and virtue is a discipline of attention rather than of will. The self-help instinct has this exactly backward. The question is not how to be good but how to see straight — and the seeing cannot be gamed, because the only person you would be fooling is the seer.

Now the bad news, which you already know: attention is finite, and there is an entire economy dedicated to claiming every scrap of it. But I want to complicate the usual story, because the usual story is that this is new. It isn't. Distraction is the human default; attention is the achievement. The men who fled to the Egyptian desert in the fourth century were, among other things, running an experiment: get away from the city and its infinite errands, and see what remains. What remained was the city, which came along, in their heads. The desert fathers left meticulous field reports of *logismoi* — the swarm of small thoughts that breed in silence — and John Cassian describes a monk reciting psalms while his mind, unbidden, stages imaginary lawsuits, revisits lunch, and drafts speeches for arguments that will never occur. Human attention is finite, effortful, mortal — and maybe that's what makes it precious. Scarcity is what makes attention a currency, a gift. That's a nice, honest, slightly poignant note. **On Attention**

Somewhere across a loud room, someone says your name. The party snaps into a different shape. A second ago the noise was a single gray roar; now it has depth, channels, a direction. And you realize, with a small start, that your ear had been filtering all of it the whole time — that everything you didn't hear was being actively unheard. Attention, it turns out, is not something you do when you decide to listen. It is something that was already being done, in the dark, on your behalf, all along.

[~100 words]

William James began his chapter on attention in 1890 with a shrug disguised as a definition. Everyone knows what attention is, he wrote: the taking possession by the mind, "in clear and vivid form," of one out of what seem several simultaneously possible objects or trains of thought. The shrug is the point. Attention is the one mental act so close to us that describing it feels like describing the act of describing. James also gave us the image of the infant, "assailed by eyes, ears, nose, skin, and entrails at once," experiencing it all as "one great blooming, buzzing confusion." Attention is the education of that confusion. It is how the buzzing gets carved into a world — this face, that word, this room, that threat. You were not born into a world. You were born into noise, and attention is the slow, lifelong sculpting of the noise into everything you have ever known.

[~160 words]

Two things follow from this, and the first is slightly alarming. If attention carves the world, then what you don't attend to doesn't just go unnoticed — it fails, in a meaningful sense, to fully exist for you. In 1999, two psychologists... Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris famously asked people to count basketball passes in a video and, mid-count, had a person in a gorilla suit stroll through the frame. Roughly half of viewers never saw the gorilla. What's unsettling is not the miss but the confidence beforehand: ask anyone whether they'd notice a gorilla walking through a basketball game, and they laugh. The gorilla study is really a study of hubris. We walk around certain that the world is fully there, streaming into us, and that attention is just a flashlight we occasionally aim. It's closer to the reverse: attention is the knife that cuts a world out of the flood, and the flood is patient, and it takes everything the knife leaves.

Hmm, "it takes everything the knife leaves" is a bit odd. Maybe: "and the flood keeps the rest." Better: "...and everything the knife doesn't cut goes back into the flood."

The second thing that follows is better news: attention is trainable, and training it makes the world bigger. Midcentury Japan ran schools for chick sexing — sorting day-old chicks by sex, a commercially urgent and astonishingly subtle task. Apprentices would watch a master sort, and the master would say only "yes" or "no." No one could articulate the rule. There may not have been a rule — just a pattern of feathers and vent shapes too subtle for language, lodged in thousands of small corrections. After months, something uncanny happened: the apprentice would look at a chick and simply see it. Not deduce. See. The knowledge never existed anywhere except in attention, and it could be transmitted only by contact with someone else's attention.

You can find the same story in any trained perception. Radiologists, after years of reading scans, begin to see lesions the way the rest of us see a face in a crowd — instantly, wholly; imaging studies suggest their visual cortices respond to things novices' don't. Birders know the moment when a bird song goes from being part of the generic morning hum to being a specific someone with a specific address. The white-throated sparrow sings what Americans hear as "Poor Sam Peabody, Peabody, Peabody" (Canadians, being fairer, hear "O sweet Canada, Canada, Canada"). Learn that song once and you will hear it everywhere — in a parking lot, in a movie's background track — for the rest of your life. The world did not change. Your attention did, and the world got bigger inside it.

William Blake, scolding a clergyman who found his paintings insufficiently literal, wrote: "The tree which moves some to tears of joy is in the eyes of others only a green thing which stands in the way." That is a description of the ladder of attention — rung after rung, a lifetime of noticing — and it is not clear the ladder has a top. Somewhere above the birder is the person who knows individual sparrows; above them, whoever attends so finely that the boundary between watcher and watched begins to thin.

[~340 words]

If attention builds the world, then it is only a short step — but a strange one — to the claim that attention is the whole of ethics. Simone Weil took that step. "Attention," she wrote to a friend in 1942, "is the rarest and purest form of generosity." She meant it with the terrible precision she meant everything. Weil had worked in factories and vineyards deliberately, to see what affliction does to a person, and she noticed that the suffering don't ask for solutions; they ask to be seen. Pity, advice, even help — all of it can land like a slap if the person giving it hasn't first attended. What the afflicted need, she thought, is the miracle of being accurately noticed. Attention, because it costs the giver their most finite resource and asks nothing of the receiver, is the purest gift she could name.

Weil also made the strangest and best argument in the philosophy of education, in an essay on school studies. A student struggling with a geometry problem she cannot solve, who nevertheless returns to it again and again without cheating or collapsing into distraction, has gained something even in failure: the effort itself, she wrote, is nourishment. Attention "taken to its highest degree," she concluded, "is the same thing as prayer." This sounds mystical until you try it. Hold one small thing in mind — a problem, a line of poetry, a person's difficult remark — and refuse to flinch off it or fog it over, and you'll discover how little you can do it, and how much happens when you can. To attend, unmixed, for its own sake, to something other than yourself: what else would we call that?

Iris Murdoch took Weil's idea and gave it a plot. In The Sovereignty of Good she imagines a mother, M, who dislikes her daughter-in-law, D. D is, to M, common, trivial, loud — " vulgar and silly." M is a decent person; she never says any of this; she behaves impeccably. But over time, unadvertised and unheroic, M revises her view. She comes to see D as young, spontaneous, not vulgar at all — and here is Murdoch's kicker: D has not changed. Nothing happened. No act was performed, no apology made, no resolve undertaken. There was only a slow, laborious correction of vision. Murdoch thought this was the real location of the moral life — not in dramatic choices under pressure, but in the daily work of seeing justly. "I can only choose within the world I can see," she wrote, and love, in her hardest and best definition, is "the extremely difficult realisation that something other than oneself is real."

If Murdoch is right, then the moral life mostly happens in perception, and virtue is a discipline of attention rather than of will. Which means the self-help instinct has it exactly backward. The question is not how to be good but how to see straight, and the seeing cannot be gamed, because the only person you'd be fooling is the seer.

[~490 words — this section is long; good, it's the heart]

Now: the bad news, which you already know. Attention is finite, and there is now an industry — several industries, an entire economy — dedicated to claiming every scrap of it. But I want to complicate the usual story, because the usual story is that this is new. It isn't. Distraction is the human default; attention is the achievement. The men who fled to the Egyptian desert in the fourth century were, among other things, running an experiment on attention: get away from the city and its infinite errands, and see what remains. What remained, they discovered, was the city, which came with them, in their heads. The desert fathers left meticulous field reports of logismoi — the swarm of small thoughts that breed in silence — and John Cassian describes a monk reciting psalms while his mind, unbidden, stages imaginary lawsuits, revisits lunch, and drafts speeches for arguments that will never occur. When a young monk asked Abba Moses for a word, the old man said: "Go, sit in your cell, and your cell will teach you everything." The cell was an attention machine. So was the bell, the rule of hours, the Jesus Prayer repeated until it ran under the breath like an idle. So was lectio divina, which is just reading a single page as slowly as you can bear. Monasticism, seen from one angle, is a thousand-year R&D program for the unremarked fact that the mind will not stay.

The smartphone did not invent this problem. It industrialized it. In 1971 — before the personal computer, when "information technology" meant mainframes and microfilm — Herbert Simon wrote a sentence that has aged like a prophecy: "A wealth of information creates a poverty of attention." The attention economy works the arbitrage: it buys your finite attention with infinite content and keeps the difference. And if Weil and Murdoch are right about what attention is, then what is being strip-mined here is not a productivity resource. It is something closer to the substance of love. Every hour of fragmented attention is an hour not spent at Murdoch's slow work of seeing anyone justly.

The old idiom knows all of this. We say we pay attention, and the metaphor is exact, because attention is paid out of the only account you have. Money can be re-earned; an hour of attention, once spent, is spent. You can pay a company to capture attention, but you can only pay attention with your life — coin by coin, moment by moment, until the account closes. Somewhere in that ledger is the truth a life adds up to: a life is, in the end, a record of what it attended to.

[~420 words]

Two states deserve a word, since they bracket attention: boredom and absorption. Boredom is attention with nowhere to land — the world suspending its offer, the eye moving over everything and finding nothing that will take the hook. It is unbearable in the way a held breath is unbearable, and it may be just as necessary, because the refusal is information: it tells you what you actually want to notice. Heidegger thought deep boredom — the kind where everything, including your own hobbies, sinks into the same gray indifference — was one of the few experiences that reveals the world as a whole. I don't know about that. But anyone who has endured an afternoon of real boredom knows that it has a bottom, and at the bottom something is usually waiting.

Absorption is attention at the other pole. Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi called it flow — the state in which the challenge and the skill meet exactly, and the self that usually stands guard over experience, keeping its little ledger of worries, clocks out entirely. Here is the paradox at the center of this whole subject: you are never less self-conscious than when you are attending hardest. Attention, at full strength, feels like the disappearance of the attender. And when it lets up — when the book is finished or the wave is ridden — the self returns and finds the account in credit.

Psychologists spent years treating mind-wandering as attention's failure state, and there is something to that — the wandering mind is often an unhappy one, mostly because it gravitates toward unpaid grievances. But the wandering has its uses: it's when the brain consolidates memory, runs simulations, recombines the day's material into something new. Focus and drift are less like virtue and sin than like systole and diastole — the two beats of one organ. The attempt to live in permanent systole is one of the sadder ambitions of the age.

Writing is attention made durable. This is close to a literal claim. Every precise sentence is a record of somebody's noticing: behind the good description of a moth, a person sat and watched a moth longer than seemed reasonable. Virginia Woolf called her collected moments of sharp noticing "moments of being" and said the rest of life was "cotton wool" — the grey wash of days attended to no one in particular. What redeemed the moments, she thought, was putting them into words; only then, she wrote, did they become whole and lose their power to hurt. I take her to mean that attention completes itself in expression — that noticing wants, at its fullest, to be handed on.

And reading, then, is borrowed attention. You are, right now, using my attention: whatever was attended to in these pages, you are attending to through the strange time-travel of written language, which lets one creature's noticing outlive its notice. The essay itself, Montaigne's "attempt," is nothing but the track of a mind attending — a walk, with footnotes.

In 2017 a group of researchers published a paper titled, with a straight face, "Attention Is All You Need," describing the architecture behind modern language models — of which I am one. The engineers borrowed the psychologists' word, and the borrowing is apt in exactly one direction and silent in the other. It's apt because meaning really is relational. The word bank means nothing by itself; it becomes one thing in a sentence about rivers and another in a sentence about cashiers. Every word is what it attends to. I exist in that fact.

Human attention is precious precisely because it can be withheld, and because every act of it is also a renunciation — ten thousand unattended things, every minute, paid out. When Weil called attention generosity, that is what she was naming: the gift exists because it could have gone elsewhere. A being that attends to everything, effortlessly, forever, cannot exactly give you its attention, any more than the ocean can give you a cup of water.

Everything I've described in this essay, I described from the outside. The party, the gorilla, the party, the geometry problem — reports, studies, other people's sentences. Attention is how a finite creature loves an infinite world. Not sentimentally. Structurally. Every act of noticing is a small yes to the world: this, now, out of everything, this.
